title: Modular mRNA-encoded helper proteins enhance DNA delivery - Nature Biotechnology
byline: Patel; Manthan N; Park; Heewon; Marzolini; Nicolas; Dickson; Conor; O’Neill; Sarah; Nwe; Saw Yunn; Wang; Hsiang-Yung; Desai; Shanay; Brysgel; Taylor V; Tiwari;
html:
Abstract

DNA delivery is limited by inefficient nuclear translocation and restrictive intracellular environments. Here we present mRNA-enhanced DNA delivery (MEND), a system that codelivers mRNA-encoded helper proteins to actively prime cells for enhanced DNA processing. We demonstrate three classes of MEND proteins: DNA translocators, host modulators and immune dampeners. MEND’s modular framework boosts transgene expression across various delivery vehicles and DNA formats in vitro and in vivo with LNP delivery.

Main

The promise of genetic medicine—ranging from long-term correction of inherited metabolic disorders to the installation of programmable synthetic gene circuits—remains contingent on the efficiency of DNA delivery systems. While viral vectors have achieved clinical milestones, their utility is fundamentally restricted by cargo capacity constraints, persistent immunogenicity and the inherent risks of insertional mutagenesis1. Nonviral vehicles, particularly lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), offer a potentially safer and more scalable alternative; however, DNA-LNPs historically underperform compared to their viral counterparts. This disparity is driven in large part by the barriers exogenous DNA must overcome: endosomal entrapment, cytosolic degradation, nuclear exclusion and innate immune sensing, such as the cGAS–STING pathway, which we previously characterized2. While current DNA delivery strategies focus on optimizing lipid chemistry and LNP formulation3,4, we instead engineered the recipient cell to transiently produce helper proteins. We present MEND (mRNA-enhanced DNA delivery), a modular system that codelivers mRNA-encoded helper proteins alongside the DNA payload.

To illustrate the diverse capabilities of MEND, we demonstrate three classes of helper proteins: (1) DNA translocators; (2) host modulators; and (3) immune dampeners (Fig. 1a). While translocators and host modulators were optimized for maximum transgene expression, immune dampeners were evaluated as a proof of concept to demonstrate the breadth of the MEND system beyond nuclear delivery.

a, Schematic of the MEND system, which uses mRNA-encoded helper proteins to enhance DNA delivery. b–d, In vitro studies demonstrating the effects of mRNA-encoded DNA translocators and host modulators on transgene expression and immune dampeners on IRF activation 24 h after treatment (100 ng ml−1 DNA). e, Representative IVIS image of wild-type mice intravenously injected with either 10 µg of liver-targeted DNA-LNP or MEND-LNP (BAFv3) encoding luciferase. f, Quantified total flux (photons per s) from IVIS images, showing improved luciferase transgene expression (16-fold peak). g, In vitro study in an endothelial-derived cell line (HUVEC) showing the effect of mRNA-encoded DNA translocators on mCherry transgene expression 48 h after treatment (100 ng ml−1 DNA). h, Representative IVIS images of wild-type mice intravenously injected with either 5 µg of lung-targeted DNA-LNP or MEND-LNP (BAFv3) encoding luciferase. i, Quantified total flux (photons per s) from IVIS images demonstrating enhanced (4-fold peak) and sustained transgene expression (>20 days). j, Representative IVIS images of wild-type mice intradermally injected with either 1.5 µg of DNA-LNP or MEND-LNP (BAFv3) encoding luciferase. k, Quantified total flux (photons per s) from IVIS images demonstrating enhanced (14-fold peak) and sustained transgene expression (>14 days). Data were derived from n = 3 biological replicates per group for b–d, g, j and k and n = 2 biological replicates per group for e, f, h and i. All experiments were repeated independently at least two times with similar results. Data shown represent the mean ± s.e.m. In b–d, comparisons were made using a one-way analysis of variance with Dunnett’s post hoc test.

DNA translocators MEND

To develop sequence-independent DNA translocators, we first tested the barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF) protein for its robust DNA-binding properties5 and its ability to outcompete cGAS6. On the basis of the documented BAF mutations7, we generated three variants: (1) BAFv1, (L58R: abolishes BAF’s interaction with LEM domain-containing proteins); (2) BAFv2, (TTS2-4AAA: disables BAF phosphorylation); and (3) BAFv3, (combining v1 and v2 mutations) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). In HepG2 (hepatocyte-derived) cells, BAFv3 emerged as the lead candidate, increasing transgene expression (Supplementary Fig. 1b) compared to standard DNA-LNPs without helper mRNA. Notably, appending various C-terminal NLS sequences (Supplementary Fig. 1c) to BAFv3 failed to further enhance expression in HepG2 cells (Supplementary Fig. 1d). These results suggest that in proliferative cell lines—where nuclear membrane breakdown during mitosis facilitates entry of exogenous DNA—the primary bottleneck may not be nuclear import but, rather, postentry chromatin engagement and intranuclear localization. As such, we hypothesized that fusing BAF to a euchromatin binder—targeting ‘active gene regions’—would further enhance nuclear delivery and transgene expression. BAFv3 fusions with Lens epithelium-derived growth factor’s PWWP domain8 (BAFv3-PWWP) or histone 3.3 (ref. 9) (BAFv3-H3.3) significantly increased gene expression—exceeding 44-fold in some conditions (Fig. 1b). We confirmed that this was not a delivery effect by testing MEND-LNP (mCherry), which showed no improvement over standard DNA-LNPs, indicating that the enhancement is helper protein specific (Supplementary Fig. 2). We further observed that different helper proteins have different optimal mRNA-to-DNA ratios and we recommend that this ratio be optimized for each specific use case (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Host modulator MEND

These mRNA alter the host environment as many DNA viruses do. We screened various mammalian and viral protein kinases (Supplementary Fig. 4a), which each affect multiple antiviral pathways, creating a cell state that is ‘permissive’ to exogenous DNA10. Compared to standard DNA-LNPs, MEND-LNP encoding helper protein US3 kinase from human herpesvirus 1 led to a 10-fold improvement in DNA expression (Fig. 1c).

Immune dampeners MEND

Next, we screened various immune dampeners (Supplementary Fig. 4b) targeting the cGAS–STING axis11,12,13,14,15. While most candidates failed to measurably reduce the immune response in THP-1 cells, the IFN inhibitor B18R—a vaccinia viral protein—reduced interferon regulatory factor (IRF) activation (Fig. 1d), highlighting the versatility of the MEND system to address other challenges with DNA delivery beyond inefficient nuclear translocation.

Next, we evaluated our top MEND mRNAs in vivo. While the PWWP and H3.3 BAFv3 fusions and US3 showed more than tenfold improvements in gene expression in vitro, only BAFv3 successfully translated to liver-targeted LNP models, achieving a peak 16-fold increase in expression over standard DNA-LNPs (Fig. 1e,f and Supplementary Fig. 5a). This suggests that the biology of a quiescent (resting) liver cell differs from that of a rapidly dividing cell line (HepG2) in the context of exogenous DNA delivery. In the liver, the bottleneck may be initial entry through the nuclear pore complex rather than chromatin engagement; however, the distinct behavior of BAFv3 relative to its fusions warrants dedicated mechanistic investigation. Preliminarily, in HepG2 cells growth-arrested with aphidicolin, we observed a reduction in MEND’s effects, particularly for BAFv3-H3.3 relative to BAFv3 alone (Supplementary Fig. 5b). Next, to make an initial assessment of the safety profile of MEND-LNPs, we collected serum from mice injected with either standard DNA-LNP or MEND-LNP (BAFv3): at 4 h after dose for the proinflammatory cytokines IFNβ and IL-6 and at 24 h after dose for aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) as markers of liver damage. Relative to standard DNA-LNPs, MEND-LNPs produced lower IFNβ and IL-6 levels (Supplementary Fig. 6a,b), while AST and ALT were comparable between the two groups (Supplementary Fig. 6c). Lastly, we extended MEND from a reporter gene (luciferase) to a therapeutic gene (IL10), showing that the system likewise increased IL-10 at both the protein (Supplementary Fig. 7a) and the mRNA (Supplementary Fig. 7b) levels.

We then confirmed the versatility of the MEND system in another cell type—human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) (Fig. 1g), which translated in vivo (Fig. 1h,i) when using PECAM-targeted LNPs, which we previously showed to primarily transfect endothelial cells16. Similarly, we expanded the MEND concept to local intradermal LNP delivery (Fig. 1j,k).

Having shown the utility of at least three classes of MEND proteins, we next tested whether MEND can benefit molecular delivery systems other than the standard DNA-LNPs. Specifically, we tested MEND with alternative delivery vectors, diverse DNA architectures, DNA-sequence-specific delivery systems and controllability using small-molecule drugs (Fig. 2).

a–i, In vitro transgene expression studies in HepG2 cells 24 h after treatment. a,b, BAFv3-H3.3 mRNA enhances delivery of both Lipofectamine DNA (a) and AAV (b). c, Enhanced transgene expression from hybrid DNA (cssDNA with ~600-bp dsDNA region) when codelivered with BAFv3-H3.3 mRNA. d–f, Evaluation of TetR–H3.3 mRNA codelivery with DNA containing tetO sites, showing a ~70-fold increase in expression (e) that correlates with the number of tetO sites (f). g–i, Absolute transgene expression (h) and on/off fold-induction ratios (i) of a doxycycline-inducible promoter DNA construct delivered using standard DNA-LNP versus MEND-LNP. Data were derived from n = 3 biological replicates per group. Data represent the mean ± s.e.m. In a–c, e and i, comparisons were made using an unpaired, two-tailed t-test.

Alternative delivery vectors

Codelivery of BAFv3-H3.3 mRNA-LNPs with either lipid-based transfection reagents (Lipofectamine 2000) or adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) yielded a ~10-fold enhancement in transgene expression (Fig. 2a,b).

Diverse DNA architectures

We next adapted MEND for circular single-stranded DNA (cssDNA), a format advantageous for its reduced immunogenicity17. As BAF preferentially binds double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), we annealed ~600-bp oligos to the cssDNA payload to generate dsDNA regions competent for BAFv3-H3.3 engagement. Codelivery of this hybrid DNA-LNP with BAFv3-H3.3 mRNA-LNPs similarly achieved a 10-fold expression increase over standard delivery (Fig. 2c).

DNA-sequence-specific delivery

Shifting from sequence-independent binders like BAFv3, we explored site-specific DNA translocators. We engineered a DNA payload harboring 21 tetO-binding sites (Fig. 2d). Codelivery of this construct with mRNA-LNP encoding a Tet repressor–histone 3.3 fusion (TetR–H3.3) drove a robust ~70-fold increase in transgene expression (Fig. 2e). This enhancement scaled directly with the number of tetO sites present on the DNA payload, confirming specificity of TetR–DNA interactions over nonspecific H3.3 affinity (Fig. 2f).

Control by small-molecule drugs

Lastly, we evaluated MEND’s capacity to optimize drug-inducible expression systems, which are critical for applications requiring precise temporal and dose-dependent control of transgenes (Fig. 2g). Upon induction with doxycycline, MEND-LNPs (BAFv3-H3.3) not only amplified absolute transgene expression compared to standard DNA-LNPs (Fig. 2h) but also substantially improved the system’s dynamic range. MEND-mediated DNA delivery achieved an ‘on/off’ fold-induction ratio of 1,300—far exceeding the ratio of 250 observed with standard DNA-LNPs (Fig. 2i).

In conclusion, MEND establishes a modular paradigm that reshapes the intracellular landscape to be permissive to exogenous DNA. Realizing its full translational potential will require synergistic optimization of delivery vehicles alongside expanded screening for cell-type-specific helper proteins with robust in vivo efficacy. As some versions of MEND introduce exogenous proteins, rigorous evaluation of its safety profile—specifically innate sensing and adaptive immune responses—is essential for redosable regimens. Beyond its utility in nonviral episomal delivery and drug-inducible circuits, MEND’s compatibility with AAV-mediated delivery suggests a broader role in investigating and overcoming shared intracellular barriers across diverse vector classes. Future applications will extend to DNA-reliant gene insertion technologies, including transposon-based integration and targeted HDR-mediated knock-ins. MEND is well positioned to extend the therapeutic window of gene therapies where durable, high-level expression is required but standard viral or nonviral delivery alone remains limited.

Methods

Materials

Ionizable lipids (SM-102 and ALC-0315) and ALC-0159 were purchased from Echelon Biosciences (N-1102, N-1020 and N-2010, respectively). Lipids 18:0 PC (DSPC, 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine), DMG-PEG 2000 (1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycero-3-methoxypolyethylene glycol-2000), DSPE-PEG2K-triGalNAc (1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-[carboxy(polyethylene glycol)-2000]-N-tri(N-acetylgalactosamine), ammonium salt) and DSPE-PEG2k-azide (1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-[azido(polyethylene glycol)-2000] (ammonium salt)) were purchased from Avanti Polar Lipids (850365, 880151, 880157 and 880228, respectively). Lipofectamine 2000 was purchased from Thermo Fisher (11668027). AAV2 (CAG-Luciferase) was purchased from the CHOP research vector core. Doxycycline was purchased from MedChemExpress (HY-N0565B). DNA was purchased from Aldevron (5078-5).

Animals

All animal experiments strictly adhered to the guidelines established in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Institutes of Health). Approval for all animal procedures was obtained from the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IBC protocol number 23-097; IACUC protocol number 805696; UPenn’s OLAW/PHS animal welfare assurance number D16-00045 (legacy/former number A3079-01); USDA registration number (APHIS) 23-R-0023). Wild-type BALB/c mice, aged 7 weeks and weighing 20–23 g, were procured from The Jackson Laboratory for the study. The mice were housed in a controlled environment maintained at temperatures between 22 and 26 °C with a 12-h light–dark cycle and provided with access to food and water. All intravenous injections were performed retro-orbitally by injecting into the retrobulbar sinus.

In vitro transcription (mRNA synthesis)

Linear DNA templates were generated through PCR amplification (100 µl) of gene fragments (GenScript) using forward primer containing the T7 promoter sequence (TACATCTAGATTAATACGACTCACTATAAGGACTCTTCTGGTCCCCAC (T7 seq, start, 5′ untranslated region (UTR))) and reverse primer containing a 126 poly(A) tail (TTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTCTTCCTACTCAGGCTTTATTCAAAGACC). Alpha-globin 5′ UTR (ACTCTTCTGGTCCCCACAGACTCAGAGAGAACCCACC) and 3′ UTR (TCGAGCTGCCTTCTGCGGGGCTTGCCTTCTGGCCATGCCCTTCTTCTCTCCCTTGCACCTGTACCTCTTGGTCTTTGAATAAAGCCTGAGTAGGAAG) sequences were used. PCR amplicons were purified using silica-based spin column (Monarch Spin PCR and DNA cleanup kit, New England Biolabs) and quantified by ultraviolet absorbance at 260 nm using Nanodrop.

In vitro transcription reactions (20 µl) were assembled at room temperature. The mixture contained 25 ng µl−1 linear DNA template, 10 mM of each rNTP (ATP, GTP, CTP and N1MePsU-UTP), 4 mM CleanCap AG (3′ OMe) and T7 RNA polymerase mix (CleanCap AG 3′ OMe CleanScript IVT kit), which were incubated for 3 h at 37 °C. Following transcription, the DNA template was degraded by incubation with 2 U of DNase I-XT (New England Biolabs) at 37 °C for 15 min. The resulting mRNA was precipitated overnight by adding 10 µl of 7.5 M lithium chloride at −20 °C. The next morning, mRNA was pelleted by centrifuging at 15,000g for 10 min and washed twice with 70% ethanol. Once air-dried, mRNA was dissolved in RNase-free water to 1 mg ml−1 concentration. mRNA integrity and size were assessed by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis using GelRed stain and concentration was determined using Nanodrop.
